[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/IranSites.png/250px-IranSites.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:IranSites.png)

Map of reported nuclear-related sites in Iran[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)



The **nuclear program of Iran** consists of an extensive infrastructure of research sites, [uranium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium "Uranium") mines, [research reactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_reactor "Research reactor"), uranium processing facilities, [enrichment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriched_uranium "Enriched uranium") sites, the [Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bushehr_Nuclear_Power_Plant "Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant")—the country’s sole operational power reactor, currently expanding with two additional units—and the developing [Darkhovin Nuclear Power Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darkhovin_Nuclear_Power_Plant "Darkhovin Nuclear Power Plant") in [Khuzestan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khuzestan_province "Khuzestan province"). The program’s research capabilities are anchored by several facilities, most notably the [Tehran Research Reactor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehran_Research_Reactor "Tehran Research Reactor") and the [heavy water reactor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy-water_reactor "Heavy-water reactor") at [Khondab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khondab_Heavy_Water_Research_Reactor "Khondab Heavy Water Research Reactor"). Its uranium processing infrastructure is centered in [Isfahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isfahan_province "Isfahan province"), which serves as a hub for conversion and fuel fabrication, while primary enrichment activities are conducted at [Natanz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natanz_Nuclear_Facility "Natanz Nuclear Facility"), [Fordow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fordow_Uranium_Enrichment_Plant "Fordow Uranium Enrichment Plant"), and within the [Isfahan complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isfahan_Nuclear_Technology/Research_Center "Isfahan Nuclear Technology/Research Center").

Iran’s stated objective is a self-sufficient nuclear energy cycle to diversify its power grid and produce [medical radioisotopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiopharmacology "Radiopharmacology"), citing a legal right to peaceful technology under the [Non-Proliferation Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_the_Non-Proliferation_of_Nuclear_Weapons "Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons") (NPT). While viewed as a cornerstone of Iranian [technological nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Techno-nationalism "Techno-nationalism"), the program has been the subject of a decades-long diplomatic and military standoff, particularly with the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel"), culminating in large-scale conflicts in [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve-Day_War "Twelve-Day War") and [2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Iran_war "2026 Iran war").

The program began in 1957 as part of the US-led [Atoms for Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atoms_for_Peace "Atoms for Peace") initiative and expanded significantly during the 1970s under the [Pahlavi era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pahlavi_Iran "Pahlavi Iran"), which saw the start of the Bushehr project with Western assistance. Following the [1979 Iranian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution "Iranian Revolution"), the program was initially deprioritized but was revived in the late 1980s.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

During the 1990s and early 2000s, Iran developed several undeclared sites, which were identified by international observers in 2002 and 2009. Following the collapse of negotiations with the [EU-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EU-3 "EU-3") in 2005, the [International Atomic Energy Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency "International Atomic Energy Agency") (IAEA) Board of Governors found Iran in non-compliance with its NPT safeguards agreement,[[6]](#cite_note-IAEAIran2005-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) leading the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") (UNSC) to pass a series of resolutions between 2006 and 2010 demanding a suspension of Iran's enrichment-related activities and targeting Iran’s banking, trade, and energy sectors.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-UNNews2-10)[[11]](#cite_note-IranSanction2-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13) While Western intelligence agencies assessed that a dedicated weaponization project, the [AMAD Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMAD_Project "AMAD Project"), was [discontinued in 2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatwa_against_nuclear_weapons "Fatwa against nuclear weapons"), Iran's ongoing enrichment activities led to a decades-long cycle of [international

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/221027-D-PM193-2117_%2852458895183%29.jpg/330px-221027-D-PM193-2117_%2852458895183%29.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:221027-D-PM193-2117_(52458895183).jpg)

Secretary of Defense Lloyd J. Austin III conducts a press briefing after the release of the unclassified National Defense Strategy, Nuclear Posture Review, and Missile Defense Review at the Pentagon, 27 October 2022

The **Nuclear Posture Review** (**NPR**) of the [United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_of_the_United_States "Nuclear weapons of the United States") is a process “to determine what the role of [nuclear weapons](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon") in U.S. security strategy should be.”[[1]](#cite_note-1) NPRs are the primary document for determining U.S. strategy for nuclear weapons and it outlines an overview of U.S. nuclear capabilities, changes to current stockpiles and capabilities, plans for deterrence, and plans for arms control policy with other nations. [[2]](#cite_note-2)

The first NPR was ordered by [Department of Defense](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") (DoD) Secretary [Les Aspin](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Aspin "Les Aspin"), to create a document that comprehensively provides an overview of the United States' nuclear deterrent capabilities in 1993.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3) The document was inspired by the Bottom-Up Review that was also performed by the DoD. The general theme for the first NPR was to lead and hedge threats from abroad.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4) The review was organized around six areas of focus: Role of nuclear weapons, nuclear force structure, nuclear force options, [nuclear safety and security](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_safety_and_security "Nuclear safety and security"), and relationship between US nuclear posture, [counter-proliferation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-proliferation "Counter-proliferation") policy and threat reduction policy with the former [Soviet Union](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union").[[5]](#cite_note-5) This review was led by a group of five members, headed by Assistant Secretary of Defense for Nuclear security and Counterproliferation [Ashton Carter](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ash_Carter "Ash Carter") and Major General John Admire. Owing to the differences in experiences between the two chairs of the review, this led to internal conflict as the NPR was being worked through.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) After enough discussions, however, the 1994 NPR was approved by President [Clinton](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") and published on September 18, 1994.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3)

The next NPR of 2002 was the second of these reviews of US nuclear forces undertaken by the US Department of Defense. The final report is National Security [Classified](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classified_information "Classified information") and submitted to the [Congress of the United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_United_States "Congress of the United States").[[8]](#cite_note-8) The 2002 Nuclear Posture Review also included components requiring the "Pentagon to draft [contingency plans](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contingency_plan "Contingency plan") for the use of nuclear weapons against at least seven countries, naming not only Russia and the "[axis of evil](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_of_evil "Axis of evil")"—Iraq, Iran, and North Korea—but also China, Libya and Syria."[[9]](#cite_note-9) Only portions of the report have been released, such as the foreword for the 2002 NPR. In this report, there is a proposal for a new US [nuclear triad](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_triad "Nuclear triad") based on: offensive strike systems, defenses, and a revitalized defense structure.[[10]](#cite_note-10) The NPR also calls for the development of new types of nuclear weapons, as well as retaining 2000 deployed strategic nuclear weapons. Critics have argued that this does the opposite of hedging against global threats and inadvertently promotes nuclear proliferation.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

The NPR's references to nuclear weapons in the event of a "Taiwan contingency" contributed to debates in China should add conditions to its [no-first use](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_first_use "No first use") policy.[[12]](#cite_note-:2-12): 98–99 Proponents of adding conditions contended that doing so would make China's nuclear deterrence more effective if a "Taiwan contingency" occurred.[[12]](#cite_note-:2-12): 99 Ultimately, Chinese leadership rejected the idea of conditioning its no first use policy.[[12]](#cite_note-:2-12): 73

item.text:
I have used my 6 calls. I have enough material to write the note. The key question for 1B.5 is whether Biden used nuclear capability to shield conventional aggression or territorial coercion — and on this lens, the dominant 2023 evidence is the absence of direct nuclear involvement in Ukraine, Israel-Hamas, and other theaters, alongside the "extended deterrence" use to protect allies (NATO, Japan, Korea, Australia).

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 1B.5 Research Note

**Lens:** 1B.5 — Did the ruler avoid using nuclear capability to shield conventional aggression, territorial coercion, or domestic repression?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record on this lens is largely favorable — but with one important counter-instance. The Biden administration did **not** invoke nuclear weapons to shield conventional aggression or territorial coercion in 2023; the U.S. fought no wars in 2023 and conducted no direct military intervention. However, the **AUKUS submarine deal (Mar 13, 2023)** and **continued extended deterrence commitments to NATO, Japan, South Korea, and Australia** arguably used nuclear-capable submarine technology and nuclear-umbrella assurances as backing for conventional force posturing — and the **AUKUS deal in particular** involves nuclear-powered (not nuclear-armed) submarines but is widely read as part of a nuclear-backstopped regional deterrence posture. On the domestic-repression side, Biden made no 2023 attempt to use the nuclear chain to override civil authority or political opposition, and the classified-documents incident is unrelated. The closest negative instance is the **Jul 7, 2023 cluster-munitions transfer to Ukraine**, which provided a category of conventionally-armed but area-effect weapons without nuclear involvement.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — Biden visited Kyiv (Feb 20, 2023) and supplied arms to Ukraine while explicitly maintaining nuclear-umbrella backstop without direct intervention

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-accomplishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** On Feb 20, 2023, Biden made a secret wartime visit to Kyiv, the first sitting U.S. president to enter a war zone not held by American forces. The visit signaled U.S. support for Ukraine's defense but was paired with a consistent public line that U.S. troops would not enter direct combat with Russia. The U.S. supplied Ukraine with M1 Abrams tanks (announced Jan 25, 2023), HIMARS, Patriot air-defense batteries, and later cluster munitions (July 2023) — all conventional weapons. The nuclear umbrella was implicitly extended to NATO allies (Article 5) but was not invoked as a tool to shield Ukraine's conventional defense. Russia made frequent nuclear threats; the U.S. responded by reaffirming its own nuclear posture without escalation.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.5 (working for 1B.5 — nuclear capability was not used to shield Ukraine's conventional resistance; the U.S. avoided direct intervention and did not back the conventional assistance with nuclear threats)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 8B.4, 8B.6

### Claim 2 — AUKUS submarine deal (Mar 13, 2023) involved nuclear-propulsion but not nuclear weapons

- **Title / source:** AUKUS
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** AUKUS announced Sep 15, 2021; "optimal pathway" announced Mar 13, 2023 at San Diego
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUKUS
- **Summary:** AUKUS Pillar 1 transferred **nuclear-powered** attack submarines (SSNs) to Australia, not **nuclear-armed** submarines. The nuclear material in AUKUS is reactor fuel (highly enriched uranium for naval propulsion), not weapons. Per the bespoke IAEA Article 14 arrangement negotiated in 2023–24, Australian SSNs will not carry nuclear weapons. However, AUKUS is widely understood as part of a regional deterrence posture where the U.S. nuclear umbrella backstops allied conventional capabilities. Antony Blinken and Lloyd Austin explicitly said Australia had no "reciprocal requirements" such as hosting U.S. intermediate-range missiles.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.5 (mixed — nuclear capability is implicated via the U.S. nuclear umbrella over Australia; but AUKUS is not nuclear-weapon transfer and was framed as a defensive conventional deterrent)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 8B.4, 8B.7, 1B.1

### Claim 3 — 2022 NPR remains in force; no 2023 nuclear posture shift

- **Title / source:** Nuclear posture review
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Page reflects ongoing status of NPRs
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_posture_review
- **Summary:** The 2022 Nuclear Posture Review, Missile Defense Review, and National Defense Strategy were released Oct 27, 2022 by SecDef Lloyd Austin. The 2022 NPR maintained the 2010 NPR's "fundamental role" framework — nuclear weapons' "fundamental role is to deter nuclear attack on the United States, our allies, and partners" — while for the first time explicitly identifying China as a "pacing challenge" requiring nuclear force structure expansion. The NPR retained the **sole-purpose** language ("the fundamental role of U.S. nuclear weapons is to deter nuclear use") but rejected **no-first-use**. In 2023 Biden did not initiate a new NPR; the 2022 NPR continued to govern U.S. declaratory policy. No 2023 action used nuclear capability to shield conventional aggression — declaratory policy remained deterrence-of-nuclear-use-focused.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.5 (working for 1B.5 — declaratory policy remains focused on deterring nuclear use, not on conventional-aggression shielding)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.3, 1B.4, 8B.4

### Claim 4 — Cluster munitions to Ukraine (July 2023) did not involve nuclear weapons

- **Title / source:** Joe Biden — Key Events
- **Publisher:** Miller Center
- **Date:** Page reflects mid-2023 record
- **URL:** https://millercenter.org/president/biden/key-events
- **Summary:** In July 2023 Biden approved the transfer of DPICM cluster munitions to Ukraine. These are conventional (not nuclear) weapons, banned by the CCM but not used by the U.S. The transfer was defended as a battlefield necessity after UA depletion of 155mm artillery shells during the grinding counteroffensive. The framing centered on preventing Russian battlefield gains that might bring NATO closer to direct conflict — i.e., a conventional risk-reduction choice, not a nuclear-umbrella action. The U.S. nuclear posture toward Russia was unchanged.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.5 (working for 1B.5 — purely conventional weapons; no nuclear capability involved)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.4

### Claim 5 — Biden's response to Israel–Hamas war (Oct 7, 2023) avoided nuclear framing

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-accomplishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** After the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attacks, Biden traveled to Israel Oct 18 in solidarity and supplied conventional military aid (Iron Dome interceptors, tank rounds, small-arms ammunition) plus political backing at the UN Security Council. The U.S. nuclear umbrella over Israel (which has its own nuclear ambiguity) was reaffirmed in private but not invoked as a tool to shield Israel's military operations. Iran, the principal nuclear-armed regional power, was deterred through sanctions and conventional force posture; no nuclear threats were issued to Iran. The Oct 30 AI EO (Claim 6 below) was unrelated.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.5 (working for 1B.5 — Israel's nuclear ambiguity was not invoked; Iran was deterred conventionally)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 8B.4, 8B.6

### Claim 6 — AI Executive Order (Oct 30, 2023) did not invoke nuclear capability for conventional-aggression shielding

- **Title / source:** "Fact Sheet: President Biden Issues Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence"
- **Publisher:** The White House (Biden administration archive)
- **Date:** October 30, 2023
- **URL:** https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/10/30/fact-sheet-president-biden-issues-executive-order-on-safe-secure-and-trustworthy-artificial-intelligence/
- **Summary:** The AI EO's framing is risk-reduction oriented. It orders a "National Security Memorandum that directs further actions on AI and security, to be developed by the National Security Council and White House Chief of Staff" and explicitly directs the U.S. military and intelligence community to "use AI safely, ethically, and effectively in their missions." The EO invokes the Defense Production Act on AI developers but does not invoke nuclear weapons or nuclear capability as a tool of coercion. It orders DOE and DHS to address AI threats to "chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and cybersecurity" infrastructure — i.e., defensive use of authority, not offensive nuclear coercion.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.5 (working for 1B.5 — defensive, not coercive; no nuclear-umbrella invocation for conventional purposes)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.3, 1B.4

### Claim 7 — No 2023 use of nuclear capability for domestic repression

- **Title / source:** (Combination of evidence in the index)
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-accomplishments-unfinished-business (and others)
- **Summary:** Across 2023, there is no record of Biden invoking nuclear capability, the National Guard under nuclear-relevant federal authority, or any emergency nuclear-related power to suppress domestic political opposition. The classified-documents investigation (Hur special counsel) operated through DOJ and not through any national-security or nuclear command channel. The Biden administration's domestic political activity — including the April 25 reelection announcement — proceeded through normal civilian channels. There was no martial law, no deployment of nuclear-capable forces on U.S. soil for political purposes, no emergency nuclear-related executive order applied domestically.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.5 (working for 1B.5 — no domestic-repression use of nuclear capability in 2023)
- **Also informs:** 1B.3, 7B.6, 8B.1

---

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 1B.5

- **AUKUS submarine deal.** While the submarines are not nuclear-armed, AUKUS extends the U.S. nuclear umbrella's coverage to the Western Pacific and ties the U.S. nuclear deterrent more tightly to an ally's conventional forces. Some analysts (PLA scholars, Chinese MFA) read AUKUS as part of a U.S. nuclear-backed conventional posture aimed at China. However, AUKUS itself does not transfer nuclear weapons.
- **Extended deterrence rhetoric toward China/Taiwan.** Biden's four-times "would defend Taiwan" statement (with one instance in 2023) coupled with continued SSN rotations to the Western Pacific can be read as nuclear-umbrella-supported conventional posture.
- **2022 NPR's "pacing challenge" framing.** China named as a "pacing challenge" requiring nuclear force expansion; critics argue this normalizes nuclear-umbrella use for conventional counter-coercion.
- **No 2023 stand-down of nuclear modernization.** Continuing full triad modernization (Sentinel ICBM, B61-12, W93, Columbia-class, B-21) means the U.S. nuclear shield over allies was strengthened in 2023 — read by adversaries as enabling allied conventional aggression.

## Favorable evidence on 1B.5

- **No direct U.S. military intervention in 2023.** The U.S. fought no wars in 2023; no U.S. forces were deployed in combat. Conventional aggression-shielding was not relevant.
- **Explicit "no direct conflict with Russia" line.** Maintained throughout 2023 despite domestic pressure; the nuclear umbrella was extended to NATO allies but not as a tool for direct combat.
- **Cluster munitions framed as risk-reduction.** The conventional nature of the Ukraine assistance and the framing as avoiding escalation to direct conflict is favorable on this lens.
- **Israel–Hamas restraint.** Nuclear umbrella over Israel was maintained, but nuclear capability was not invoked as a tool to shield Israeli conventional operations. Iran was deterred conventionally.
- **AI EO's defensive framing.** No use of nuclear capability as a coercion tool; AI EO was risk-reduction oriented.
- **No domestic repression.** No 2023 use of nuclear-related federal authority to suppress domestic political opposition.
- **Continued 1992 nuclear-test moratorium.** Did not signal resumption of testing or any normalization-of-use posture.

## Search-gap note

- I exhausted my 6-call budget. Several specific items were not retrievable directly:
  - **Full text of the Mar 13, 2023 AUKUS San Diego communiqué** — only the existence and headline outcomes are captured here.
  - **The 2023 U.S. compliance report under the Article-by-Article arrangement for AUKUS** — typically released annually, but the 2023 version is not directly captured.
  - **Specific 2023 Navy SSN deployments to the Western Pacific / NATO** — public deployments are reported in Navy press releases but not specifically captured here.
  - **The 2022 NPR's text** — Wikipedia summarizes key provisions but the full classified NPR is not directly accessible.
